courses.title: MATHEMATICAL ANALYSIS 1
courses.description: Numerical sets: real numbers, ordering and completeness; complex numbers: algebraic and trigonometric form, De Moivre theorems, n-th roots. Real functions of one real variable: domain, codomain, graph; elementary functions; composition of functions, invertibility and inverse function; monotonic, symmetric, periodic functions; sequences. Limits and continuity: main properties, indeterminate forms, rate of growth, monotone convergence, Weierstrass theorem, intermediate value theorem. Derivative: derivation rules, applications, differential and linear approximation, Fermat, Lagrange, De L'Hospital theorems; higher order derivatives; Taylor's formula, local approximation by polynomials, convex functions, maxima and minima, graph of functions. Integral of one variable functions: definite integral, main properties and applications; primitives, fundamental theorem of calculus, integration rules. Curves in R3. Numerical series; Taylor' series. Complex exponential function.

courses.title: FUNDAMENTALS OF COMPUTER SCIENCE
courses.description: Overview of computers and programming: functional description of an elementary computer, algorithms, programming languages, compilers, operating systems and networks. Encoding of the information, boolean operators and fundamental theorems. Programming language concepts using the C or C++ language: data abstraction and the use of types, control structures for the execution of a sequence of statements. Top-down design with functions, parameter passing among functions, local and global variables and the recursive programming. File management using operating system services. Translation of C or C++ programs into assembly language. Introduction to system programming.

courses.title: GEOMETRY AND LINEAR ALGEBRA
courses.description: Vectors. Analytic geometry in cartesian 2 and 3 dimensions. Matrices; linear maps and systems; eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Euclidean spaces Rn. Conics and quadric surfaces.

courses.title: PHYSICS
courses.description: Physical quantities and measurements.. Kinematics of a point particle. Newtonian dynamics, forces, study of motion. Work and energy. Dynamics in non-inertial reference frames. Elementary interactions between masses and electrical charges. Dynamics of particle systems and rigid bodies. Elements fluid mechanics Thermodynamical systems. The first end the second principles of thermodynamics. Kinetic theory of gases.

courses.title: BASIC CIRCUIT THEORY
courses.description: Introduction to basic electric quantities. Kirchhoff Laws. Resistive one-port elements. Element constraints. Electric Power. Solution of simple circuits. Two-port elements. Controlled sources. Special two-port elements. Matrix representation. Analysis of resistive circuits: general methods, superposition principle. Thevenin and Norton equivalent one-ports. Dynamic components: capacitors, inductors, coupled inductors. Linear first order dynamic circuits (RC and RL). Sinusoidal steady state: phasor analysis, impedance and admittance, power, applications (resonance, maximum power transfer, impedance matching, power factor). Elementary three-phase circuits. Magnetic circuits (magnetic flux, reluctance) and real transformers. Electromagnetic fields theory: electrostatic fields and slow time-varying fields. Faraday's law and Ampere's law (integral form). Gauss' law. Conservation of charge.

courses.title: FUNDAMENTALS OF INTERNET AND COMMUNICATION NETWORKS
courses.description: The course will focus on Internet architectures and communication technologies. The students will learn how and why the Internet works like it does, further going into the details of the design choices the Internet is based on. The course will follow an "hands-on" approach building up on several practical examples to let the students see how theoretical concepts are working in practice. Always in the hands-on spirit, software tools for network design and performance evaluation will be used throughout the course. The course will start off by presenting the foundations of computer networks and communication protocols, moving then to some fundamental principles of communication systems; the student will learn how the information is "manipulated" in order to be transferred through the Internet and which are the metrics used to evaluate the performances of a communication systems and a communication network in general. The Internet protocol stack will be illustrated using a top-down approach, starting from the application layer (the most visible to the final user) and then going down through the transport layer, the network layer and the network access layer. The last part of the course will be dedicated to private networks and Intranets

courses.title: MATHEMATICAL ANALYSIS 2 (FOR STUDENTS IN INFORMATION ENGINEERING)
courses.description: Real functions of two or several variables: limits, continuity, level curves and surfaces, gradient, differentiability and linear approximation, higher order derivatives, Taylor's formula; free optimization; constrained optimization, Lagrange multipliers. Linear differential equations: 1st order and 2nd order equations, superposition principle, structure of general solution, existence and uniqueness for the initial value problem, solution techniques. Fourier series: pointwise convergence, amplitude spectrum. Double and triple integrals: properties and applications, formulae of reduction, change of variables (polar, cylindrical, spherical coordinates). Curves in the space: regularity, tangent straight line, normal plane. Line integrals: length of a curve, work of a vector field, conservative vector fields, potential function. One topic between a) Surfaces in R3: area, surface integrals, flow of a vector field through a surface; curl and divergence theorems in the plane and in the space. b) Differential linear systems: structure of general solution, existence and uniqueness for the initial value problem.

courses.title: COMPUTER ARCHITECTURES AND OPERATING SYSTEMS
courses.description: Parallel and concurrent programming models: processes and threads. The structure of Operating Systems: process management, virtual memory, file system structure and device drivers. Introduction to digital logic circuits: Boolean algebra and lgic gates, boolean function implementation and basic combinational circuits, basic sequential elements, memory organization. Functional subsystems: buses and interfacing. Processor microarchitecture: data path and control path, microcode. Microarchitecture design and performances: pipelining and cache memory. Instructution Set Architectural level (with a reference processor): instruction formats and addressing modes, assembly process and linking.

courses.title: LOGIC AND ALGEBRA
courses.description: Relations and maps: Relations of arity 2, properties and closure of a relation with respect to a given set of properties. Equivalence relations and partitions, quotient set. Order relations. Surjective, injective and bijective maps, existence of the inverse map, kernel, factorization theorem of maps. Cardinality: Cantors theorem. Algebraic structures: definitions, examples and elementary properties of main algebraic structures, substructures, congruence relations, quotient structures, homomorphisms. Propositional logic: well formed formulas and semantic, formal systems. Deduction, soundness and completeness theorems. First order logic: the language of first order logic, terms and well formed formulas. Semantic and models. Prenex normal form. Formal systems: soundness and completeness. Examples of first order theories.

courses.title: ELECTROMAGNETICS AND FIELDS
courses.description: The course presents the fundamental concepts of the behavior of electromagnetic fields at the base of the functioning of the main ICT applications. The physical laws regulating electromagnetic fields in invariant (static) regime and showing possible applications are described. Introduce and comment on Maxwell's equations describing electromagnetic interactions in a variant time regime on a non-microscopic scale. Examples of application of the theoretical laws to the study of electromagnetic wave transmission in free and guided space are presented, with particular attention to the most important applications in the ICT field. The teaching introduces to a good level of mathematical formalism that facilitates a complete study of electromagnetic fields and their applications.

courses.title: PROBABILITY AND STATISTICS FOR COMPUTER SCIENCE
courses.description: The course is organized in two parts. The first part concerns the basic elements of probability theory: axiomatic definition of probability space, conditional probability, independence, random variables and random vectors (joint distributions, moments, Gaussian vectors, covariance matrix, ...), Law of Large Numbers and Central Limit Theorem. In the second part the basic concepts of mathematical statistics are given: elements of the theory of parametric point estimation (maximum likelihood method and moment method), confidence intervals for population characteristics, hypothesis tests, hints of non-parametric statistics. The course topics will be carried out with attention to stimulate a double vision of the basic themes: from the points of view of mathematical models and of engineering applications. The aim of the course is to provide the student with the conceptual bases both to face applications in the field of Computer Engineering in the presence of random phenomena, and to afford the study of the probabilistic/statistical issues present in advanced courses.

courses.title: THEORY OF STOCHASTIC PROCESSES
courses.description: Information theory studies the fundamental limits related to information representation and transmission. The course introduces the fundamentals of probability and random processes seen through the lenses of information theory and its main applications in the field of computer and communications engineering. In addition to basic concepts of probability and random processes, the course will introduce the concepts of entropy, relative entropy, mutual information and their application to data compression, the source coding, data transmission, computational complexity, probabilistic inference. The course also addresses the basic concepts of estimation and numerical simulation of random experiments, both essential as a tool for the analysis and design of modern computer and communication systems. The laboratory activity will focus on the construction of simulation models in MATLAB with the objective to apply and verify the theory studied during the lessons.

courses.title: SIGNALS AND SYSTEMS FOR COMMUNICATIONS
courses.description: Continuous and discrete signals: the step and impulse signals, complex exponentials, elementary operations on signals. ; Continuous and discrete Linear Time-Invariant systems: the impulse response, convolution. ; Representation of signals in the frequency domain: Fourier transform of continuous-time signals, Fourier transform of sequences, Fourier series. ; From continuous to discrete time: the sampling theorem, energy and power of sampled signals, conversion to base-band by sampling, sampling in the frequency domain. ; The discrete Fourier transform (DFT): circularity in time and frequency, properties, practical applications. ; Continuous and discrete random processes: power spectral density, processes through LTI systems. ; Source coding: quantization, binary coding, Hufman coding, Entropy of the source. ; Digital transmission in base-band: PAM and PCM, interference between symbols, matched filter, probability error.

courses.title: ALGORITHMS AND PRINCIPLES OF COMPUTER SCIENCE
courses.description: Computer science models. Automata, grammars, Petri Nets, applications of mathematical logic to system modeling. Theory of computation. Church`s thesis; unsolvable problems. Computational complexity. Computational models and relations between their computational complexities. Linear acceleration. Algorithms and data structures. Order of magnitude of computational complexity; searching and sorting; fundamental data structures: stacks, queues, trees, hash tables. Backtracking, Divide et impera. NP-completeness.

courses.title: FUNDAMENTALS OF AUTOMATIC CONTROL
courses.description: Control problems: an overview (control objectives, basic structures and terminology, primary features, performance evaluation). Mathematical models of physical systems. Oriented systems (dynamic vs. non dynamic systems, time-invariant vs. time-varying systems, linear vs. nonlinear systems; state variables and normal form, equilibrium conditions, linear model tangent to a system at an operating point). Analysis of linear time-invariant systems in the time-domain (state-motion and output-response, superposition of effects, stability of motion, stability of system, stability criteria). Elements of signal analysis: main transforms and their properties. Analysis of linear time-invariant systems in the frequency-domain (state-motion and output-response, superposition of effects, transfer function, cancellations and Kalman canonical decomposition (hint), system stabilizability, realizations of a transfer function, block diagrams, stability analysis of systems described by a block diagram, frequency response, system bandwidth). Performance evaluation of linear feedback control systems: (robust, asymptotic) stability criteria, phase and gain margins, dynamic precision (bandwidth and sensitivity, load and output disturbances, measurement and transmission errors), static (asymptotic) precision, periodic disturbances. Try and error techniques for control system design. Linear (PID) and nonlinear (switching) industrial regulators. Tuning rules. Non elementary control architectures (feedforward vs. feedback, cascade control, decoupling). Digital control (hints).

courses.title: GENERAL CHEMISTRY
courses.description: Basis concepts: elements and compounds, chemical formulae, mole, simple reactions, stoichiometry. Atomic structure: nucleus and electrons. Electronic structure of atoms and the periodic system. The chemical bond: Ionic bonding: crystal structure and properties of ionic compounds. Covalent bonding: molecules and covalent solids. The metallic bond: conductors and semiconductors. States of matter: description of the gaseous state by the ideal-gas equation of state and of solids and liquids by phase diagrams. Chemical thermodynamics: First and second principles of thermodynamics. Enthalpy, entropy and Gibbs free energy state functions, and their application to the calculation of the heat, spontaneity and equilibrium conditions of chemical reactions. Chemical kinetics: reaction rate. The molecular collision model of chemical reactions. Parameters affecting reaction rates. Catalysts. Reactions and equilibria in aqueous solutions: Acids, bases and acid-base equilibria. Autoprotolysis of water and the pH. Red-ox reactions. Electrochemical cells, electromotive force, standard reduction potentials, electrolysis.

courses.title: THERMODYNAMICS AND HEAT TRANSFER
courses.description: Fundamentals of Thermodynamics: First Law for closed and open systems: internal energy and enthalpy. Second Law for closed and open systems: entropy. External and internal irreversibilities. Applied thermodynamics: turbine, pump, heater and cooler. Analysis of power generation and refrigeration systems. Heat transfer. Conduction: The Fourier law. Unidirectional steady conduction. Extended surfaces (Fins). The lumped capacitance model for unsteady conduction. Convection: basic principles of convection: forced and natural convection. Dimensional analysis and model theory. Correlations in forced and natural convection. Radiation: black body radiation. Heat transfer between black surfaces. Diffuse-gray surfaces. Application: heat exchanger, electronic cooling.

courses.title: MEASUREMENTS
courses.description: Metrology: principles of measurements; reference standards and International System of units (SI); fundamental and secondary measurement units; units in linear and logarithmic scales; graphic representation of experimental data. Statistical analysis of measurement data: probability density function, mean, variance, correlated variables, and measurement uncertainty; compatibility between measurements and weighted mean value. Interpolation and regression of measurement data. Data acquisition systems: sampling and A/D conversion; characteristics and working principles of DACs and ADCs (speed, resolution, quantization uncertainty, number of equivalent bits); properties and use of DAQ systems; LabVIEW software for automated measurements. Instrumentation: digital voltmeters (differential and integrating) and multimeters (DMM); digital oscilloscope; basics of spectral measurements and spectrum analyzers. Applications: A couple of specific examples of measurements will be discussed in detail during exercises and experimentally verified during the Lab. activities.

courses.title: ELECTROMAGNETICS AND TRANSMISSION MEDIA
courses.description: The course covers the basic principles of electromagnetism necessary to deeply understand the various types of transmission media typically used in ICT. The course starts with a survey on time-dependent electromagnetic fields, Maxwell's equations, propagation and radiation of electromagnetic waves. Then, the most common transmission media are considered: copper wires and cables (twisted pairs), optical fibers, waveguides, antennas and propagation of waves in free space (WiFi). The requirements from the signal transmission point of view, properties, potentials and limits of transmission media are presented and compared in the actual applicative scenario in the ICT. The emphasis is on physical phenomena and applications.

courses.title: INTRODUCTION TO ELECTRONICS
courses.description: The course provides the students with a basic understanding both of electronic circuits (analog and digital) and of devices. Topics covered in the subject include: - Signals: acquisition and processing; sources and sensors; time domain and frequency domain analysis. - Circuits: transfer function, amplification and attenuation, input and ouptput impedance, circuit cascading. - Electronic devices: semiconductors, pn-junction diode, MOS transistor. - Digital electronics: CMOS logic, volatile and non-volatile memories. - Analog electronics: MOS single-stage amplifiers, MOS differential stage, operational amplifier, negative feedback, inverting and non-inverting amplifier, input and output impedance, current conveyors, summer, differential amplifiers, integrators, differentiators, frequency response and stability. - Analog to digital conversion: sampling theorem, sample&hold circuits, A/D converters, D/A converters. The focus of the subject is twofold: both understanding the basic concepts that drive the operation of an electronic circuit and understanding the impact of non-idealities of real components on the circuit performances. This course is not intended to develop a specific skill in electronics, but rather to give the student a rather broad view of the overall aspects of electronics. The breadth of topics covered in this course makes it useful both for the students who intend to graduate after the first three years and for the students who want to specialize in the field of electronics.

courses.title: INFORMATION SYSTEMS (FOR STUDENTS IN INFORMATION ENG.)
courses.description: Introduction to information systems: classification of information systems, evolution of information systems. Operational information systems, transactional information systems. Introduction to ERP, and CRM systems. Cooperative and distributed information systems. Business Processes Modelling (BPM). Support to process execution: technologies based on workflow management systems and on Web services. Life cycle and information system planning. Introduction to security of information systems: principles of cryptography; applications of information systems and electronic signature; data security; security plan.

courses.title: DATA BASES 1
courses.description: This course aims at communicating to students two basic abilities: designing and querying databases. After a brief introduction dedicated to data models and formal languages for databases, the course turns to the description of relational systems. Using SQL both as a query and data manipulation language, we show its use as a means for delivering relational applications. Next, we illustrate the Entity-Relationship model as an instrument for conceptual database design, discussing how the design process takes place and the quality requirements of design results.

courses.title: BUSINESS ECONOMICS AND ORGANIZATION
courses.description: Firms: objectives, typologies, ownership and control. General accounting: functions, content and classification of financial statements; liquidity and profitability. Long-run decisions (investment analysis): cost of capital, cash flows, Net Present Value, other assessment methods. Analysis of markets: demand, cost structure, perfect competition, other market structures. Cost accounting: cost typologies, cost analysis and allocation, short-run decisions, budgeting. Business organization: definitions, elements of organization design. Examples and applications from the ICT industries.

courses.title: INFORMATION SYSTEMS
courses.description: Introduction to information systems: classification of information systems, evolution of information systems. Operational information systems, transactional information systems. Introduction to ERP, and CRM systems. Cooperative and distributed information systems. Business Processes Modelling (BPM). Support to process execution: technologies based on workflow management systems and on Web services. Life cycle and information system planning. Introduction to security of information systems: principles of cryptography; applications of information systems and electronic signature; data security; security plan.
learning_outcomes: The student: - knows the fundamental principles, generalizations, theories, and concepts of the components that constitute an information system (DdD 1); - knows the issues related to the evolution of an information system to build a resilient and innovative system (DdD 1); - is able to apply the acquired knowledge to model business processes for information processing and design the architecture of an information system (DdD 2).

courses.title: DATABASES
courses.description: The primary objective of the course is the acquisition of two basic skills: to design databases and to extract information from them formulating complex queries. After a brief introduction on data models and formal languages for databases, the course focuses on relational databases, with SQL as a fundamental tool, in the dual role of a language for the definition and for the manipulation of data, also in combination with other technologies within applications that use relational data. The course then describes a theoretical framework for conceptual modeling of application domains, with the Entity-Relationship model as a reference. Conceptual modeling is considered within the bigger picture of a design process that goes from the initial requirements analysis to the implementation of a suitable relational schema, through various design phases and techniques that take into account the quality requirements that must characterize the results of each phase.

courses.title: ECONOMICS & BUSINESS ADMINISTRATION
courses.description: Firms: objectives, typologies, ownership and control. General accounting: functions, content and classification of financial statements; liquidity and profitability. Long-run decisions (investment analysis): cost of capital, cash flows, Net Present Value, other assessment methods. Analysis of markets: demand, cost structure, perfect competition, other market structures. Cost accounting: cost typologies, cost analysis and allocation, short-run decisions, budgeting. Business organization: definitions, elements of organization design. Examples and applications from the ICT industries.
learning_outcomes: Students are expected to acquire knowledge of the different types of firms, their operating mechanisms, objectives, and the context in which they operate. They will understand the key elements of organisational design, innovation dynamics, the criteria guiding short-term and long-term business decisions, the tools of internal and external accounting, the corporate budgeting process and performance evaluation mechanisms, as well as the main market forms and the factors influencing market demand and supply.
Students will be able to evaluate investment projects, prepare and assess financial statements, analyse short-term decision making, and develop a basic assessment of performance results.

Students will develop the ability to understand the main mechanisms governing firm behaviour and to use the basic tools of internal and external accounting, useful also to increases their entrepreneurial attitudes.

courses.title: DIGITAL LOGIC DESIGN
courses.description: This subject has the goal of introducing the student to the logic design of digital circuits and systems, considering basic problems and methods. Logic synthesis and design optimization are treated, starting from combinational networks and then considering sequential systems, even complex ones. Merit figures of the optimization process are defined, valid also for the case of adoption of CAD based methods.Prototyping and/or implementation of digital systems will be examined adopting field programmable logic gate arrays (FPGA).

courses.title: SOFTWARE ENGINEERING
courses.description: Software Design: Object-Oriented design. Client-server architectures and distributed programming in Java, Event-based component interaction and GUI design. Unified Modeling Language: Description of a software architecture in UML. UML for requirements analysys and specification. Software Testing: Goals, foundations, techniques. Software Life-cicle: Software process and software evolution. Configuration management.

courses.title: SYSTEMS THEORY (NONLINEAR DYNAMICS)
courses.description: The basic elements of nonlinear dynamics (stability, bifurcation theory, catastrophes) are presented, in order to provide some tools for the analysis of complex systems. The theoretical notions are illustrated with the aid of examples taken from various fields of science and engineering. The main topics of the course are: Asymptotic behaviors in nonlinear systems: equilibria, cycles, tori, and strange attractors. Liapunov stability. Structural stability. Local and global bifurcations. Catastrophic bifurcations. Numerical methods for bifurcation analysis. Applications to collective dynamics and to slow-fast systems.

courses.title: INDUSTRIAL AUTOMATION
courses.description: The course provides the methodological and practical foundations for the management of automation and control problems related to industrial machines and plants. Techniques for modeling, analysis and control of discrete event systems are studied in detail. Some real case studies of industrial processes are also discussed, with focus on flexible manufacturing systems.

courses.title: FOUNDATIONS OF HUMAN-COMPUTER INTERACTION
courses.description: This teaching aims to introduce the principles and methodologies for the design of interactive systems that, in addition to being functional, possess qualities with impact on end users and are therefore effective, efficient and satisfying with respect to the tasks that users must complete through the systems. Such design involves the application of people-centered processes that can guide the construction of user interfaces that take into account the needs and characteristics of users, the nature of the tasks they will need to accomplish through the system, and the environment in which the system will be used. The course will therefore focus on these processes and introduce the following content: Interaction models, interaction paradigms, usability of user interfaces, User Experience Principles for interaction design, visual design and design patterns. User-centered design: The human-centered desing model and iterative design. Context analysis and user analysis. Methods of gathering user requirements. Methods of prototyping. Usability evaluation methods. Accessibility and inclusiveness of interactive systems.

courses.title: FOUNDATIONS OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
courses.description: The goal of the course is to introduce the students to basic problems, models, and techniques of Artificial Intelligence (AI), and to enable them to model and solve specific AI problems. The course covers the most fundamental concepts, modelling approaches, and resolution methods of classical AI, and also provides an introduction to the history of the discipline and to some philosophical issues involved. The course also briefly overviews some AI topics that are discussed in depth in other courses. The teaching method is traditional (classroom lessons).
learning_outcomes: Students will become acquainted to:
· the types of problems that are tackled in AI
· the types of applications that can profit from the use of AI-based solutions
· basic AI modelling and problem-solving techniques
· crucial moments in the history of AI
· critical issues involved in the effort of mechanising intelligent processes
Students will learn to:
· analyse and model problems according to different AI approaches
· design specific problem-solving techniques as instances of general classes of techniques
· evaluate the complexity of different modelling and problem solving techniques in connection with particular problems
Students will become able to appreciate the relevance and possibility of developing and applying AI methods in different application fields of industrial relevance
Students will be able to understand and critically evaluate AI systems deployed in different application scenarios

courses.title: BIOINFORMATICS ALGORITHMS
courses.description: Bioinformatics is an increasingly important and interesting area of computer science application. This discipline was born from the growing need in Molecular Biology to develop adequate computational tools for the resolution of multiple problems, including those derived from the analysis of biological sequences (DNA, RNA, proteins). In particular, the recent biotechnologies of next generation sequencing enable to generate precise, but also very big, data of biological sequences, which raise complex problems and require specific algorithms for their effective and efficient processing and computational analysis. The course aims to introduce the students to such problems and to their computational solution, with the main goal to provide the algorithmic knowhow to successfully face both the study and the efficient solution of a variety of problems regarding sequences, trees and graphs in Bioinformatics. It will develop the skills to design exact or approximated algorithms for the solution of optimization problems regarding sequences, trees and graphs which are used to solve Bioinformatics problems, and the ability to use software available in the Internet for the study of biological sequences.
learning_outcomes: Students will learn how to:
- Align two or more sequences to each other (global and local sequence alignment, multiple sequence alignment)
- Align short sequences produced by modern sequencing technology to a reference genome (read mapping)
- Assemble a genome from short sequences produced by modern sequencing technology (genome assembly)
- Model functional biological sequences by means of Hidden Markov Models
- Identify differences in a sequenced genome with respect to a reference genome (variant/mutation calling)
Given specific biological sequences (e.g., DNA sequences such as next-generation sequencing reads, reference genomes) students will be able to:
- Perform global and local sequences alignments
- Apply Burrows-Wheeler transformations on genome sequences and use the transforms to perform exact and inexact matching of short sequences
- Understand the complexity of sequence analysis algorithms and discard inefficient algorithms
- Understand how functional sequences can be modeled by statistical means using a Hidden Markov Model
Given the discussion of multiple alternative approaches and underlying concepts, students will learn to:
- Evaluate the appropriateness of an algorithm based on its complexity as well as the complexity of the task
- Appreciate the importance of algorithms that approximate an optimal solution
Given the discussion of multiple alternative approaches and underlying concepts, students can:
- Learn to approach the same algorithmic problem in different ways and from different (sometimes opposing) starting points
- Learn to what aspects pay attention when studying a specific approach (e.g., time and space complexity, inexact versus exact solutions)

courses.title: FUNDAMENTALS OF NUMERICAL ANALYSIS
courses.description: Errors in Numerical Processes: Stability and conditioning of numerical methods and algorithms. Numerical Solution of Linear Systems: Condition number and its influence on errors propagation. Direct methods: Gaussian elimination and matrix factorizations. Iterative procedures: Jacobi, Gauss Seidel, S.O.R. Solution of overdetermined linear systems by the Least-Squares method. Eigenvalues Approximation: The power method and the QR method. Solution of Nonlinear Equations: Iterative methods: bisection method, fixed-point iteration and Newton method for system of nonlinear equations. Zeros of polynomials. Approximation: Polynomial interpolation. Splines interpolation. Least-Squares approximation and data fitting. Numerical Integration: Newton-Cotes rules. Composite rules. Adaptive quadrature. The Solution of the Cauchy Problem for Ordinary Differential Equations: One step methods, Euler, trapezoidal rules and Runge-Kutta methods. Stability and convergence analysis. MATLAB software library.

courses.title: PROJECT IN COMPUTER SCIENCE AND ENGINEERING
courses.description: The course aims at providing to students a way to practice about some of the knowledge acquired along the various study courses, through the realization of a practical project, under the guidance of a teacher who proposes the theme and is in charge. The pre-requisites are indicated project by project; in general, the knowledge of at least one programming language among those used in the courses (or the availability to learn it during the project) is required.

courses.title: ROBOTICS
courses.description: Robot as a system: component parts; functional model of a robot; robot versus robotics; the operator place (telecontrol, autonomous behaviour). Mechanics: degrees of mobility and freedom; links, joints, wheels and steering; classification of mechanical structures; Cspace. Controlling movements and contacts: geometrical and physical entities; kinematics and dynamics; Cartesian and actuation space; controller using the robot model and trajectory computation; controller using external sensors; control problems in mobile robots. Programming: programming tasks in Cartesian space; simulators and virtual reality for user interface. Assigning tasks to robot: reactive and deliberative architectures; robots as physical agents and the co-ordination problem. World immersion and sensors: kind of sensors and their use as proprioceptive and eteroceptive; sensorial fusion; the role of learning. Images and vision: image acquisition and analysis; from computer vision to robot vision; vision for user interface. Maps, sensors, odometers in mobile robots: path planning; autolocation and natural landmarks.
learning_outcomes: Students will learn:
· What are the main type of mobile robot kinematics and their characteristics in terms of direct and inverse kinematics equations
· How to structure the autonomous navigation system of mobile robots and autonomous vehicles
· What are the classical method for trajectory planning, i.e., graph and sample based, and the most common algorithms for trajectory planning
· What are the most common algorithm for trajectory following and obstacle avoidance
· What are the most used techniques for localization, mapping and simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM)
· What are the common sensors used in robot perception, their pros and cons, their use for autonomous navigation and mapping
· The Robot Operating System (ROS) framework and how it can be used in the development of autonomous robots
Given a specific domain design for a mobile robot, the student will be able to:
· Design the system architecture for the autonomous navigation of the robot, its modules, and their algorithms
· Implement the software system controlling a modern autonomous robot based on the ROS middleware
· Design and develop SLAM algorithms for simultaneous localization and mapping
· Derive the kinematic equation for a mobile robot, develop the corresponding odometry system and integrate its outcome into a localization or SLAM system
Given an autonomous robot design problem, students will be able to:
· Identify the proper kinematics for the robot to be developed
· Identify the proper sensors the robot should have to fulfill its task
· Select the most appropriate algorithms for trajectory planning and trajectory following
· Select the most appropriate approach for SLAM, localization or mapping
The student will learn to:
· Discuss in written form the pros and cons of different kinematics in the realm of a specific design problem
· Describe the learned algorithms in written form, discussing their pros and cons.
Student will learn to:
· Face the design of the software system for an autonomous robot with a sound background and well defined patterns
· Develop the software controlling an autonomous robot/vehicle based on the ROS middleware and simulate it under Gazebo

courses.title: INFORMATIC TECHNOLOGIES FOR THE WEB 1
courses.description: Network and system programming: TCP/IP network programming, parallel programming, development of client/server distributed applications. Introduction to the structure of Operating Systems, with reference to Linux: processes description, control and management, memory management and virtual memory, file system structure and device drivers. Structured computer organization: levels and virtual machines. Digital logic level: logic gates and Boolean algebra, Boolean functions implementation, basic combinational circuits, basic sequential elements, memory organization. Functional subsystems, buses and interfacing: bus organization and bus arbitration, memory and I/O devices interfacing, interrupt handling. Microarchitecture level: the data path e control path of the IJVM machine, microinstructions and microcode, microarchitecture design and performances: pipelining and cache memory. Instruction Set Architecture Level: instruction formats, instruction types and addressing modes, IJVM memory model and operand stack, IJVM instruction set, assembly process and linking.

courses.title: THERMODYNAMICS AND HEAT TRANSFER
courses.description: Fundamentals of Thermodynamics: First Law for closed and open systems: internal energy and enthalpy. Second Law for closed and open systems: entropy. External and internal irreversibilities. Applied thermodynamics: turbine, pump, heater and cooler. Analysis of power generation and refrigeration systems. Heat transfer. Conduction: The Fourier law. Unidirectional steady conduction. Extended surfaces (Fins). The lumped capacitance model for unsteady conduction. Convection: basic principles of convection: forced and natural convection. Dimensional analysis and model theory. Correlations in forced and natural convection. Radiation: black body radiation. Heat transfer between black surfaces. Diffuse-gray surfaces. Application: heat exchanger, electronic cooling.

courses.title: MECHANICS
courses.description: The first part of the course is dedicated to the study of the kinematics of the rigid bodies in plane motion with geometry and algebra of vector solutions and complex numbers method. Arguments such the phenomenon of the contact between solids, as friction are introduced. The second part of the course deal with the dynamics of rigid bodies system in plane motion. General equations of dynamics are discussed and is introduced the D`Alambert principle. Work-Energy relations are treated in the study of the energy flow in a machine with the characterization of engine, transmission and utilizator. Concepts of steady and transient rate, direct and retrograde motion are discussed. For all the arguments the development of various numerical applications are provided.

courses.title: TRANSMISSION AND COMMUNICATION DEVICES
courses.description: This course presents the main devices used for the generation, transmission and detection of information in the areas of widest interest in information and communication technologies. The physical principles and the electromagnetic aspects underlying the operation of sources, modulators, filters, amplifiers and receivers operating at radiofrequency and optical frequencies are introduced, and the photonic and microwave technologies currently used for the realization of these devices are illustrated. The main issues related to guided wave (metal and dielectric waveguides) and radiated (antennas) electromagnetic fields are discussed, and their exploitation for the implementation of passive and active devices is presented. The course illustrates the characteristic parameters and the functional scheme of the presented devices, together with the requirements for their use in data transmission systems. Particular attention is given to issues related to energy consumption and to the scaling up of the amount of information, pointing out the theoretical, technological and physical limits. The overall goal of the course is to provide a comprehensive overview of the transmission technologies employed for interconnections, from very short to very long distances.

courses.title: INTRODUCTION TO INTERCONNECTING TECHNOLOGIES
courses.description: The course provides an overview of available interconnection technologies by delving into their classification and aspects. The course provides quantitative tools for analyzing the performance of interconnection technologies; the student then learns to critically analyze interconnection systems being then able to design and size different systems according to specific application areas and supported services. Part of the course also covers an introduction to radio standards for IoT (short and long range) preparatory to specialized courses on pervasive systems and IoT.

courses.title: OPTICS AND IMAGING
courses.description: The course aims to provide the basics of contemporary optics and to present the principles and technologies related to optical images. Starting from Fourier diffraction theory and optics, optical systems for image formation and filtering will be analyzed. Examples of image acquisition and reproduction systems will also be introduced

courses.title: INVERSE PROBLEMS APPLIED TO REMOTE SENSING
courses.description: The course aims to present the theoretical and practical foundations necessary to process data acquired from an arbitrary sensor system in order to extract information of interest. The proposed program is intended to be preparatory with respect to all topics related to numerical data analysis addressed in the Master's degree courses. At the same time, great emphasis will be given to specific examples taken from the world of electromagnetic remote sensing, intended to give an understanding of the practical use of the methods in application contexts. All topics of the course will be presented both with traditional lectures and with a hands-on approach, through which students will learn to solve complex problems by numerical computation and to interpret the results.

courses.title: NETWORK SECURITY
courses.description: The aim of the course is to introduce security aspects in communication networks and the Internet, providing a broad overview of cryptography protocols and systems for secure communication on the network. After an introduction to the theoretical bases of cryptography and the theory of numbers (mathematics of integers or discrete mathematics), the most important encryption algorithms are presented both symmetric and based on public key. Then, authentication methods and protocols are presented for messages and users, based on hash functions, electronic signatures, Challenge and Response protocols, passwords, certificates, as well as protocols for establishing and distributing encryption keys. Finally, protocols for the security of communication on the Internet, at the application, transport, and network level are illustrated. The course will be enriched by monographic seminars on specific network security issues, held by industry experts or telecommunications operators. All course topics are addressed by providing the necessary mathematical theoretical culture, but always emphasizing the practical and applicative aspects of greater relevance.

courses.title: SOFTWARE DEFINED NETWORKING
courses.description: The aim of the course is to present to the student the basic characteristics and objectives of the software defined networks (abstractions, interfaces, use cases) providing the basic notions on network automation through the creation of simple network applications in emulated environment and in a laboratory environment. Finally, the course gives the rudiments of programming a network operating system and the use of the northbound and southbound interfaces.
